overview: A channel is a typed conduit through which goroutines send and receive values, created with `make(chan T)`; it is Go's primary mechanism for communication and synchronization between concurrent tasks.

An unbuffered channel is synchronous: a send `ch <- v` blocks until another goroutine executes a matching receive `v := <-ch`, and the receive blocks until a send is ready. The two operations happen at the same moment — a rendezvous.

Channels embody Go's motto: 'Don't communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating.' Beyond passing data, channel operations establish happens-before guarantees that make concurrent code safe without explicit locks.
learningObjectives: Create unbuffered channels with `make(chan T)` and perform send/receive operations.
Explain why an unbuffered channel is a synchronous rendezvous and what happens-before guarantee it provides.
Use the comma-ok receive `v, ok := <-ch`, `close(ch)`, and `for v := range ch` correctly, following the rule that the sender closes.
Multiplex multiple channels with `select`, add non-blocking behavior with `default`, and add timeouts with `time.After`, while recognizing deadlocks and nil-channel behavior.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: A channel is a typed, first-class, reference-typed synchronization primitive that provides a FIFO queue of values shared between goroutines; an unbuffered channel has zero capacity, so every send is paired one-to-one with a receive and the two goroutines synchronize at the point of exchange.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think of an unbuffered channel as a hand-off with no table in between: the sender holds out a value and waits until a receiver is there to take it directly. Neither side proceeds until both are ready, so the channel both moves the data and coordinates the timing.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Channels come from Tony Hoare's Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP, 1978) and Rob Pike's earlier languages Newsqueak, Alef, and Limbo. Go made channels a first-class, typed language feature backed by the runtime, pairing them with goroutines so that CSP-style message passing became the idiomatic way to write concurrent programs.

whyItMatters.business: Channels let services coordinate concurrent work safely, turning multi-core hardware into higher throughput without the subtle race bugs that cause outages and lost revenue.
whyItMatters.engineering: They replace error-prone shared-memory locking with explicit message passing, making concurrent pipelines, fan-out/fan-in, and cancellation easy to reason about and review.
whyItMatters.scalability: Channels provide natural backpressure: a slow consumer blocks fast producers on an unbuffered channel, so the system self-regulates instead of building unbounded queues.
whyItMatters.cost: Correct synchronization via channels avoids the debugging cost of heisenbugs and the runtime cost of over-coarse locking, getting more useful work per CPU.
whyItMatters.reliability: Channel operations carry happens-before guarantees in the Go memory model, eliminating a whole class of data races that are otherwise the top source of concurrency bugs.

coreComponents.name: Channel value (hchan)
coreComponents.definition: A reference to a runtime hchan struct holding the queue, wait queues, and a lock; created by make(chan T).
coreComponents.purpose: Carry typed values between goroutines and synchronize them.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Track element type, buffer (if any), waiting senders/receivers, closed flag, and a mutex.

coreComponents.name: Send operation
coreComponents.definition: The statement `ch <- v` that transmits a value into the channel.
coreComponents.purpose: Hand a value to a receiver (and, on unbuffered channels, synchronize).
coreComponents.responsibilities: Block until a receiver is ready (unbuffered); panic if the channel is closed.

coreComponents.name: Receive operation
coreComponents.definition: The expression `<-ch`, optionally `v, ok := <-ch`, that takes a value out of the channel.
coreComponents.purpose: Receive data and detect channel closure.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Block until a value is available; return the zero value with ok=false when closed and drained.

coreComponents.name: close(ch)
coreComponents.definition: The built-in that marks a channel as closed, signalling no more values will be sent.
coreComponents.purpose: Tell receivers the stream has ended.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Wake all blocked receivers; subsequent sends panic; closing again panics.

coreComponents.name: select statement
coreComponents.definition: A control structure that waits on multiple channel operations, proceeding with one that is ready.
coreComponents.purpose: Multiplex channels, add timeouts, and do non-blocking I/O.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Choose a ready case (uniformly at random if several); run default if none ready.

coreComponents.name: Element type and direction
coreComponents.definition: The T in chan T, plus optional directional types chan<- T (send-only) and <-chan T (receive-only).
coreComponents.purpose: Type-check values and restrict how a channel may be used.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Enforce that only T flows through and that APIs expose only the intended direction.

internalWorking: make(chan T) allocates a runtime hchan struct on the heap and returns a reference (pointer) to it, which is why channels are passed by reference and the zero value of a channel variable is nil.

hchan contains a circular buffer `buf` (used only by buffered channels), the element size/type, a `closed` flag, two wait queues `recvq` and `sendq` (linked lists of parked goroutines wrapped in sudog structs), and a `lock` protecting all of it.

On an unbuffered send, the runtime locks the channel; if a receiver is already parked in recvq, it performs a direct send — copying the value straight from the sender's stack into the waiting receiver's variable — then unparks the receiver. No buffering happens.

If no receiver is waiting, the sending goroutine wraps itself in a sudog, enqueues onto sendq, releases the lock, and parks; a future receiver finds it, copies the value, and unparks it. The symmetric logic applies to a receive that arrives first.

close(ch) sets the closed flag and wakes every goroutine in recvq (they get the zero value, ok=false) and sendq (those panic). All of this happens under the channel lock so the transitions are atomic with respect to other channel ops.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: sender: ch <- v --> [lock hchan] --> receiver parked in recvq? --(yes)--> direct copy v into receiver var, unpark receiver --(no)--> enqueue sender on sendq, park | receiver: <-ch --> [lock hchan] --> sender parked in sendq? --(yes)--> copy value, unpark sender --(no)--> enqueue on recvq, park | close(ch) --> set closed, drain recvq with zero/false, panic any sendq
dataFlowWalkthrough: main creates ch := make(chan string) — an unbuffered channel with zero capacity.
main launches `go worker(ch)`; the worker computes a result and executes `ch <- result`.
If main has not yet reached `<-ch`, the worker parks in sendq holding the value; if main is already waiting, the value is copied directly.
main executes `v := <-ch`; the runtime pairs the send and receive, copies the value, and unparks whichever goroutine was waiting.
Because the send completed before the receive returned, everything the worker did before the send is now visible to main (happens-before), and both goroutines continue.

keyTerminology.meaning: A channel with capacity 0 where each send must rendezvous with a receive.
keyTerminology.importance: Guarantees synchronization, not just data transfer.

keyTerminology.meaning: The synchronized meeting point where a send and receive complete together.
keyTerminology.importance: Defines the blocking semantics of unbuffered channels.

keyTerminology.meaning: The memory-model ordering: a send happens-before the corresponding receive completes.
keyTerminology.importance: Why channel-passed data needs no extra locks to be visible.

keyTerminology.meaning: `v, ok := <-ch`, where ok is false once the channel is closed and drained.
keyTerminology.importance: The reliable way to detect closure.

keyTerminology.meaning: A channel marked done by close(); receives return zero values immediately, sends panic.
keyTerminology.importance: Signals end-of-stream to all receivers at once.

keyTerminology.meaning: A channel variable that was never made; sends and receives on it block forever.
keyTerminology.importance: Used to disable a select case dynamically.

keyTerminology.meaning: A state where all goroutines are blocked; the runtime aborts with a fatal error.
keyTerminology.importance: The classic failure mode of misusing unbuffered channels.

importantConcepts.concept: Synchronization is the point, not a side effect
importantConcepts.explanation: On an unbuffered channel the send and receive happen together. This makes a channel both a data pipe and a synchronization barrier — often you send a value purely to coordinate timing (e.g. a done signal).

importantConcepts.concept: The sender closes, never the receiver
importantConcepts.explanation: Only the goroutine(s) producing values know when there are no more. A receiver closing the channel could cause a producer's later send to panic. The convention is: the owner/sender closes, and only once.

importantConcepts.concept: Closing is a broadcast, sending is one-to-one
importantConcepts.explanation: A single value sent goes to exactly one receiver, but closing wakes every blocked receiver simultaneously, which is why close() is the idiom for broadcasting a 'stop' to many goroutines.

importantConcepts.concept: Receiving from a closed channel never blocks
importantConcepts.explanation: After a channel is closed and drained, every receive returns the element type's zero value immediately with ok=false — which is exactly what makes `for range ch` terminate.

variationsAndTypes: Unbuffered channels (capacity 0) — synchronous rendezvous; the focus of this lesson.
Buffered channels (make(chan T, n)) — sends only block when the buffer is full; covered in depth in the sibling lesson.
Directional channels (chan<- T send-only, <-chan T receive-only) — compile-time restrictions for safer APIs; covered alongside buffering.
Signal/done channels (chan struct{}) — carry no data, used purely to notify or broadcast via close.
Nil channels — block forever, used to switch off a select case at runtime.
advantages: Provide synchronization and data transfer in one primitive, with memory-model happens-before guarantees.
Make concurrent ownership of data explicit, avoiding shared-memory data races.
Unbuffered channels give natural backpressure: producers can't outrun consumers.
compose cleanly with select for timeouts, cancellation, and multiplexing.
disadvantages: Easy to deadlock: a send with no ready receiver (or vice versa) blocks forever and the runtime aborts.
Misuse panics: sending on or closing a closed channel, or closing a nil channel.
Unbuffered hand-offs are slower than a plain mutex-guarded variable for trivial sharing.
Goroutines blocked on channels with no peer leak silently.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: When goroutines must exchange data or coordinate timing — pipelines, fan-out/fan-in, signalling completion or cancellation, and any place you want a happens-before guarantee without manual locking.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: For simple protected counters or flags where a sync.Mutex or sync/atomic is cheaper and clearer, or for hot paths where the synchronous hand-off overhead dominates.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: An unbuffered channel is like a relay-race baton pass: the incoming runner (sender) can't let go until the outgoing runner (receiver) has a hand on the baton, and the outgoing runner can't start until the baton arrives. The exchange forces them to meet at the same instant — that meeting is the rendezvous. close() is the race official blowing the whistle to tell everyone the heat is over.

commonMisconceptions.myth: An unbuffered send returns as soon as the value is 'in the channel'.
commonMisconceptions.reality: There is no storage; the send blocks until a receiver takes the value directly.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You should close every channel when done, like a file.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Closing is only needed to signal receivers; many channels are simply garbage-collected unclosed. Closing is a signal, not cleanup.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Receiving from a closed channel panics or errors.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It returns the zero value with ok=false immediately and forever; only sending on a closed channel panics.

commonMisconceptions.myth: select runs the first ready case in source order.
commonMisconceptions.reality: If multiple cases are ready, select picks one uniformly at random to avoid starvation.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Use unbuffered channels for backpressure when you want producers throttled by consumers; switch to bounded buffered channels only when you need to absorb bursts.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Always give a blocked goroutine an escape — pair channel ops with context cancellation or a done channel in a select so they can't leak.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Guard against panics from sending/closing closed channels by making one owner responsible for the channel's lifecycle and closing exactly once (sync.Once if needed).
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Track goroutine count; goroutines stuck on channel sends/receives show up as steady NumGoroutine() growth and in goroutine profiles as parked on chansend/chanrecv.
productionConsiderations.security: Treat channels as the synchronization boundary — never share the underlying data after sending it, so a value has a single owner at a time and can't be mutated concurrently.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Avoid spawning a goroutine plus channel for trivial synchronization; a mutex or WaitGroup is cheaper. Reserve channels for genuine data flow.
productionConsiderations.performance: An unbuffered hand-off costs a park/unpark and a copy; on hot paths batch values or use a small buffer instead of one element per rendezvous.

codeExamples.title: Unbuffered send/receive as a synchronization point
codeExamples.overview: A worker goroutine computes a result and sends it on an unbuffered channel; main blocks on the receive until the value arrives, demonstrating the rendezvous.
codeExamples.breakdown: make(chan string) builds an unbuffered channel. The worker's `ch <- result` cannot complete until main reaches `<-ch`, and main's receive cannot complete until the worker sends — they meet at the same instant. The directional type `chan<- string` documents that worker only sends. No WaitGroup is needed: the receive itself is the synchronization.
codeExamples.commonIssues: If main never receives (e.g. you remove `<-ch`), the worker blocks forever; if you forget `go` and call worker(ch) directly, main deadlocks on the send since no receiver exists yet.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: When you only need a 'finished' signal and not data, use `chan struct{}` and send/close it — struct{} occupies zero bytes.

codeExamples.title: Producer closes, consumer ranges (with comma-ok)
codeExamples.overview: A producer sends a stream of integers then closes the channel; the consumer drains it with `for range` and the comma-ok form shows what closure looks like.
codeExamples.breakdown: produce sends 1, 2, 3 then calls close(out). The `for v := range ch` loop receives each value and exits cleanly when the channel is closed and empty — no sentinel value needed. The final `v, ok := <-ch` shows the post-close behavior: an immediate zero value (0 for int) with ok=false. The sender, not the consumer, owns closing.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
got 1
got 2
got 3
after close: v=0 ok=false
codeExamples.commonIssues: Closing from the consumer side, or sending after close, panics with 'send on closed channel'; ranging over a channel that is never closed deadlocks once the producer stops.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use the comma-ok form only when you need to distinguish a real value from closure; `for range` is cleaner for simple draining.

codeExamples.title: select for multiplexing, timeout, and non-blocking receive
codeExamples.overview: Combine two data channels, a timeout via time.After, and a default case for a non-blocking poll using select.
codeExamples.breakdown: The first select has a default, so it returns immediately when no channel is ready — a non-blocking receive. The loop's select blocks on a, b, or a 100ms timeout. a fires at ~50ms (received), then b is still pending at the 100ms deadline so time.After wins and prints a timeout. If several cases were ready at once, select would pick one at random.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
nothing ready yet
received from a
timeout waiting for a value
codeExamples.commonIssues: Calling time.After inside a long-running loop allocates a new timer each pass (use time.NewTimer/Ticker for tight loops); a select with only a default never blocks and can busy-spin.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: To disable a case dynamically, set its channel variable to nil — a nil channel never becomes ready, so select simply ignores that case.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A log-ingestion service must read parsed log lines from a producer, process them one at a time downstream, and shut down cleanly when the source is exhausted or a deadline is hit — without dropping lines or leaking goroutines.
endToEndExample.inputData: A stream of parsed log-line strings emitted by an upstream parser goroutine, of unknown total length.
endToEndExample.architecture: A single unbuffered channel `lines chan string` connects the parser (producer) to the processor (consumer in main). A `select` in the consumer also watches a timeout channel so an idle source can't hang the service.
processingSteps: main creates an unbuffered channel `lines := make(chan string)`.
Launch the parser goroutine which sends each parsed line on `lines` and calls close(lines) when the source ends.
In main, loop with a select over `<-lines` (with comma-ok to detect closure) and `<-time.After(deadline)`.
On each received line, process it; the unbuffered channel ensures the parser pauses while the processor is busy (backpressure).
When the comma-ok receive reports ok=false, the channel is closed and drained — exit the loop cleanly; if the timeout fires first, abort and report.
endToEndExample.output: Each log line is processed exactly once in order, and the service exits with a clear reason: 'source closed' or 'timed out'.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Expose processed-line count and goroutine count; a stuck parser shows up as a goroutine parked on chansend and a flat processed counter.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: The consumer treats ok=false as orderly end-of-stream; the timeout case handles a stalled producer; the producer is the sole owner that closes the channel exactly once.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Backpressure from the unbuffered channel keeps memory flat, closure signals completion without a sentinel, and the timeout guarantees the service never blocks forever — no dropped lines, no leaked goroutines.

industryUseCases.problem: Streaming build and container events to consumers as they happen.
industryUseCases.solution: Unbuffered/lightly-buffered channels hand events from producers to a consumer that the channel close signals as finished.
industryUseCases.benefits: Ordered delivery with natural backpressure and a clean end-of-stream signal.

industryUseCases.problem: Coordinating goroutines and reacting to shutdown across controllers.
industryUseCases.solution: A closed `struct{}` 'stop' channel broadcasts cancellation; select combines work channels with the stop channel.
industryUseCases.benefits: One close() reliably wakes every waiting goroutine to shut down.

industryUseCases.problem: Fanning scrape results into processing while limiting in-flight work.
industryUseCases.solution: Channels connect scrape producers to consumers, using select with timeouts to bound slow targets.
industryUseCases.benefits: Throttled, race-free pipelines that degrade gracefully on slow endpoints.

industryUseCases.problem: Passing messages between connection goroutines without shared-memory races.
industryUseCases.solution: Typed channels move messages between goroutines as the synchronization boundary.
industryUseCases.benefits: High concurrency with memory-model-safe hand-offs instead of locks.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Unbuffered channels self-throttle producers to consumer speed; when you need to absorb bursts, introduce a bounded buffer (sibling lesson) rather than removing the backpressure entirely.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Designate one owner per channel responsible for closing it exactly once; wrap close in sync.Once if multiple paths could trigger it, to avoid 'close of closed channel' panics.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Use a shared, closed-once 'done'/stop channel inside select cases so every goroutine can be drained on deploy or shutdown without leaks.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Make consumers idempotent so that a restart which reprocesses in-flight values (lost in an unbuffered hand-off during a crash) does not double-apply effects.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Each unbuffered exchange costs a goroutine park/unpark plus a copy; for high-rate streams, batch multiple items per send or add a small buffer to amortize the synchronization cost.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Don't pair a goroutine and channel for trivial coordination — a mutex/WaitGroup is cheaper; reserve channels for genuine data flow and signalling.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Transfer ownership of the data with the value: once sent, the sender must not touch it, so the receiver is the sole accessor and concurrent mutation is impossible.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Watch goroutine profiles for goroutines parked on chansend/chanrecv — a growing count indicates senders or receivers with no peer (a leak or deadlock-in-waiting).
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Use the comma-ok receive to distinguish a real zero value from a closed channel so consumers never mistake closure for valid data.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log the reason a select loop exits (closed vs timeout vs cancellation) and alert on timeout rates and rising goroutine counts that signal stalled channels.

recommendedPractices: Let the sender (channel owner) close the channel, and close it exactly once.
Use `for v := range ch` to drain until close, and comma-ok only when you must detect closure mid-loop.
Pair every potentially-blocking channel op with a cancellation/timeout path in a select to prevent leaks.
Prefer unbuffered channels by default for the synchronization guarantee; add buffering only with a measured reason.
engineeringStandards: Run tests with -race; even channel-based code can have races in surrounding shared state.
Expose channels through directional types (chan<- T / <-chan T) at API boundaries.
Never send on or close a channel you do not own.
designRecommendations: Give each channel a single, clearly documented owner responsible for its lifecycle.
Use `chan struct{}` for pure signalling and close() to broadcast to many receivers.
Combine work channels with a done/context channel in select for clean shutdown.
namingConventions: Name channels after the values they carry (lines, jobs, results, errs).
Name signal channels done, stop, or quit; declare them as chan struct{}.
documentationStandards: Document who closes each channel and under what condition.
State the channel's direction and whether it is buffered in the API doc comment.
testingStrategies: Use timeouts (select with time.After) in tests so a deadlocked channel fails fast instead of hanging.
Assert that ranging over a channel terminates, proving the producer closes it.
Check NumGoroutine() returns to baseline to catch goroutines leaked on channel ops.

commonMistakes.mistake: Sending on an unbuffered channel with no receiver.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Calling the producer synchronously instead of in a goroutine, or all goroutines blocked.
commonMistakes.impact: fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Ensure a receiver is running concurrently (start producer or consumer with `go`).

commonMistakes.mistake: Closing a channel from the receiver side.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Treating close() like cleanup the consumer should do.
commonMistakes.impact: A later send by the producer panics with 'send on closed channel'.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Only the sender/owner closes; the receiver just stops receiving.

commonMistakes.mistake: Closing a channel twice (or closing a nil channel).
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Multiple shutdown paths both call close.
commonMistakes.impact: panic: close of closed channel / close of nil channel.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Close exactly once, guarding with sync.Once when several paths can trigger it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Ranging over a channel that is never closed.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Producer forgets to close after the last send.
commonMistakes.impact: Consumer blocks forever; deadlock if it is the last goroutine.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Always close the channel when production is complete.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mistaking a received zero value for valid data after close.
commonMistakes.impact: Processing a phantom zero value as if it were real.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use comma-ok or range to detect closure.

comparisonSection.explanation: Channels transfer ownership and carry happens-before guarantees; mutexes guard in-place shared state. Channels favor data flow; mutexes favor protecting a small piece of shared state.
Unbuffered sends block until a receiver is ready (full synchronization); buffered sends only block when the buffer is full, trading the rendezvous for capacity (covered in the sibling lesson).

Closing a channel broadcasts a stop to all receivers and composes with select; context wraps that pattern with deadlines and propagation across API boundaries and is preferred for request-scoped cancellation.
A plain receive waits on exactly one channel; select waits on several at once, supports a timeout case and a non-blocking default, at the cost of more syntax.

beginnerQuestions.question: How do you create an unbuffered channel and send/receive on it?
beginnerQuestions.answer: `ch := make(chan T)` creates it; `ch <- v` sends and `v := <-ch` receives.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Tests the basic syntax and that capacity defaults to 0 (unbuffered).

beginnerQuestions.question: What does it mean that an unbuffered channel is synchronous?
beginnerQuestions.answer: A send blocks until a receiver is ready and a receive blocks until a sender is ready; they complete together as a rendezvous.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Checks understanding of blocking semantics, the core of unbuffered channels.

intermediateQuestions.question: What does `v, ok := <-ch` return after the channel is closed?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Once closed and drained, it returns the element type's zero value with ok=false, immediately and forever.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Tests closure detection and the comma-ok idiom.

intermediateQuestions.question: Who should close a channel and why?
intermediateQuestions.answer: The sender/owner, because only it knows when no more values will be sent; a receiver closing it could make a later send panic.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Probes the ownership convention that prevents close-related panics.

advancedQuestions.question: What happens if you send on a closed channel, close a closed channel, or operate on a nil channel?
advancedQuestions.answer: Sending on a closed channel panics; closing a closed or nil channel panics; sending or receiving on a nil channel blocks forever (useful to disable a select case).
advancedQuestions.explanation: Tests deep knowledge of channel edge cases and the runtime panics.

advancedQuestions.question: Explain the happens-before guarantee of channel operations.
advancedQuestions.answer: In the Go memory model a send on a channel happens-before the corresponding receive completes (and a close happens-before a receive that observes the channel as closed), so writes before the send are visible after the receive without extra locks.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Tests memory-model understanding underpinning race-free channel use.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A program prints 'fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!' on a line that sends to an unbuffered channel.
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: An unbuffered send needs a concurrent receiver; if every goroutine (including main) is blocked, the runtime detects deadlock.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: There is no goroutine ready to receive — likely the producer was called synchronously instead of with `go`, or the consumer exited early. Start the producer or consumer in a separate goroutine, or add a receiver, so the send can rendezvous.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a fan-in that merges results from several worker goroutines into one ordered consumer that shuts down cleanly.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Each worker sends on a shared results channel; a coordinator uses a WaitGroup to know when all workers are done and then closes the channel; the consumer ranges over it. A done/context channel in a select lets the whole thing cancel early.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Unbuffered keeps memory low but couples worker speed to consumer speed; a small buffer decouples them at the cost of backpressure.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Bound worker count, add buffering sized to burstiness, and shard channels per consumer if a single consumer becomes the bottleneck.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: An unbuffered channel (make(chan T)) is a synchronous, typed conduit where each send rendezvous one-to-one with a receive.
keyConcepts: make(chan T) = unbuffered; send `ch <- v` and receive `v := <-ch` block until paired.
v, ok := <-ch: ok is false once the channel is closed and drained.
The sender closes, exactly once; close broadcasts to all receivers.
Receiving from a closed channel returns zero/false immediately; sending on it panics.
select multiplexes channels; default = non-blocking, time.After = timeout.
formulas: unbuffered send completes  ⇔  a matching receive is executing (rendezvous)
send happens-before corresponding receive completes (memory model)
commands: go run -race main.go        # catch races around channel use
go tool pprof http://host/debug/pprof/goroutine  # find goroutines parked on chansend/chanrecv
interviewPoints: Send on closed channel panics; receive returns zero/false.
nil channel send/receive blocks forever (disables a select case).
quickNotes: for v := range ch ends when ch is closed and drained.
Deadlock = all goroutines asleep; the runtime aborts.
Use chan struct{} for pure signalling.
select picks randomly among ready cases.

keyTakeaways: An unbuffered channel created with make(chan T) is a synchronous rendezvous: a send blocks until a receiver is ready, providing both data transfer and a happens-before synchronization guarantee.
Detect closure with `v, ok := <-ch` or `for v := range ch`; receiving from a closed channel yields the zero value with ok=false, while sending on a closed channel panics.
The sender owns and closes the channel exactly once; closing broadcasts 'no more values' to every receiver at once.
select multiplexes multiple channels and adds non-blocking (default) and timeout (time.After) behavior; misusing channels causes deadlocks and panics, so always give blocked goroutines an escape.
